key_parameters.value: 5 sigma clipping threshold in immoments; inclination i = 20.5 deg from axis ratio; D = 1.5 x a_maj; v_circ = 0.75 FWHM / sin(i)

evidence.quote: We made an intensity-weighted mean velocity map and a velocity dispersion map (Figure 5), using the CASA task `immoments` with a conservative $5\sigma$ clipping to avoid noisy pixels.

The inclination angle of the disk ($i=20\ensuremath{^\circ}.5$, where $0\ensuremath{^\circ}$ is face-on) is determined from the axis ratio of the deconvolved size. claims.hypothesis: The broad [C II] wing in J1243+0100 is driven by a galactic-scale quasar-driven neutral outflow that will soon quench star formation in the host galaxy.
claims.experiment: Fit the area-integrated [C II] spectrum with a double Gaussian, measure the wing spatial extent in the uv plane, check for companions and merger kinematics, and compute outflow mass, rate, mass loading factor, kinetic power, and momentum load.
claims.result: The broad wing has FWHM = 997 +/- 227 km s^-1, spatial extent < 2.7 kpc (3 sigma), atomic outflow rate > 447 +/- 137 M_sun yr^-1 (total outflow rate >= 1410 M_sun yr^-1), and mass loading factor >= 9 relative to SFR_[CII] (or >= 5 relative to SFR_cons_TIR).
claims.finding: The broad wing is the first detection of a galactic-scale quasar-driven outflow at z > 7, and its large mass loading factor indicates it will soon quench host star formation.

evidence.quote: This wing is the first detection of a galactic-scale quasar-driven outflow (atomic outflow rate $> 447~M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$) at $z > 7$. The estimated large mass loading factor of the total outflow (e.g., $\gtrsim 9$ relative to the \[C II\]-based SFR) suggests that this outflow will soon quench the star-formation of the host.

evidence.loc: Nature of the broad wing component
evidence.quote: We thus conclude that the broad \[C II\] wing is due to a *fast neutral outflow*.

claims.hypothesis: The cold gas kinematics of the J1243+0100 host galaxy are dominated by ordered disk rotation with a central massive bulge.
claims.experiment: Perform 3D tilted-ring kinematic modeling of the [C II] cube with 3DBarolo and fit the extracted radial rotation velocity profile with a spherical Plummer potential.
claims.result: The rotation-to-dispersion ratio is V_rot / sigma_disp ~ 3-5 across all rings, and the centrally rising rotation curve is well fit by a Plummer potential with M_bulge = (3.3 +/- 0.2) x 10^10 M_sun and scale radius a = 0.36 +/- 0.03 kpc.
claims.finding: The host galaxy dynamics are rotation-dominated and suggest that a massive compact bulge has already formed at z ~ 7, although this bulge estimate is tentative due to limited spatial resolution.

evidence.quote: The radial velocity is 3–5 times larger than the velocity dispersion in all bins, clearly indicating that the gas dynamics of J1243$+$0100 is *rotation-dominated*.
Our current data therefore suggests that a massive bulge has already formed in this system at $z \sim 7$. However, our resolution is limited, thus this estimate of $M_{\rm bulge}$ is *tentative*.

claims.hypothesis: Low-luminosity quasars at z ~ 7 already follow the local black hole-to-host mass co-evolution relation.
claims.experiment: Compare the Mg II-based black hole mass of J1243+0100 with both the thin-disk dynamical mass M_dyn and the dynamically modeled bulge mass M_bulge against the local Kormendy & Ho (2013) relation.
claims.result: J1243+0100 has M_BH / M_dyn ~ 0.4% and M_BH / M_bulge ~ 1%, both consistent with the local relation within uncertainties.
claims.finding: The black hole-host co-evolution relation is already in place at z ~ 7 for this low-luminosity quasar, whereas optically luminous z > 6-7 quasars appear over-massive likely due to selection bias.

evidence.quote: Finally, we found that J1243$+$0100 has a black hole mass-to-dynamical mass ratio (and -to-bulge mass ratio) of $\sim 0.4\%$ ($\sim 1\%$), consistent with the local value within uncertainties. Our results therefore suggest that the black hole-host co-evolution relation is already in place at $z \sim 7$ for this object.

evidence.quote: Therefore, sensitive observations of lower luminosity objects, even at $z>7$, are necessary to gain a less-biased picture of early SMBH/galaxy evolution.

why_this_method.value: Fitting visibilities in the uv plane avoids deconvolution uncertainties when separating point-source and extended emission; extracting the spectrum within the 2 sigma contour of the moment-0 map yields lower noise than a circular aperture for resolved complex sources.

evidence.quote: Doing this fit in the $uv$ plane avoids uncertainties in the deconvolution process (cite: 2015ApJ...810..133I; 2017ApJ...835..286I; 2019ApJ...887..107F; 2020ApJ...900....1F).
This method gives lower noise than measurement within a circular aperture, particularly when the source is resolved and complex (cite: 2020A&A...643A...2B).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Single Gaussian fit to the [C II] line spectrum, rejected due to poor fit (chi^2/d.o.f = 50.1/27) compared to a double Gaussian fit (chi^2/d.o.f = 16.5/25).

evidence.quote: Given this broad component, the spectrum is poorly fit with a single Gaussian (Figure 4a, Table 2) with a returned $\chi^2$/d.o.f = 50.1/27 (estimated over $\pm 1000$ km s$^{-1}$). A double Gaussian fit (Figure 4b, Table 2), both centered on the same frequency, gives much better results: $\chi^2$/d.o.f. = 16.5/25.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Close companion galaxies or merger-induced shocks as the origin of the broad [C II] wing, rejected due to lack of detected companions within 3'', symmetric line profile, compact wing size (<0''.52), and rotation-dominated host kinematics.

evidence.quote: It could be due to (A) close companion/merger galaxies or (B) fast \[C II\] outflows (cite: 2021arXiv210101199I). However, we do not consider cenario (A) to be likely for a number of reasons

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Starburst-driven outflow as the origin of the broad [C II] wing, rejected because the mass loading factor (>= 5-9) and velocity extent (~900 km s^-1) exceed typical starburst-driven values.

evidence.loc: Nature of the broad wing component
evidence.quote: It is also rare for starburst-driven neutral outflows to reach velocities greater than $\sim 500$–600 km s$^{-1}$ even for ULIRG-class objects (cite: 2005ApJ...621..227M; 2005ApJS..160..115R; 2018MNRAS.473.1909G; 2020A&A...633A..90G), whereas the observed \[C II\] profile of J1243$+$0100 extends to $\sim 900$ km s$^{-1}$. Thus we conclude that the fast \[C II\] outflow of J1243$+$0100 is *quasar-driven*.

evidence.quote: The core gas dynamics are governed by rotation, with a rotation curve suggestive of a compact bulge ($\sim 3.3 \times 10^{10}~M_\odot$), although it is not yet spatially resolved.
However, our resolution is limited, thus this estimate of $M_{\rm bulge}$ is *tentative*.

referee_caveats_inferred: The 3DBarolo tilted-ring model fits 6 rings separated by 0''.1 across a radius of 0''.6, which heavily oversamples the 0''.70 x 0''.56 beam; the inner rotation curve and inferred compact bulge mass may be strongly affected by beam smearing and fixed inclination/center assumptions.
Both M_dyn and M_bulge rely on small inclination angles (20.5 deg and 25 deg), where sin(i) corrections amplify any axis-ratio measurement errors.
The double Gaussian spectral fit forces the broad wing to share the exact systemic velocity center of the narrow core, which could bias the wing flux and width if the outflow is asymmetric.
